opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underrated frictions in the whole intelligence explosion story. The naive picture is that you get a model that's a really good AI researcher, it comes up with a better algorithm, and then instantly you have a smarter model. But in practice, most algorithmic improvements don't transfer for free to the model you already have. If you discover a better architecture or a better data mixture, you often need to train a new model from scratch to realize the gains, and each generation is more expensive than the last. So there's a real compute and wall-clock bottleneck baked into every turn of the loop.

That said, I don't think it kills the idea. A few things push the other way. First, a lot of progress can be validated at small scale. Much of what researchers do today is run experiments on small models, look at scaling curves, and only commit the big run once they're confident. If you have automated researchers who are much better at that, with better research taste, fewer wasted experiments, and faster iteration, you compress the time between big runs even if the big runs themselves don't get cheaper.

Second, not everything requires retraining from scratch. Post-training, RL, better scaffolding, better inference-time compute: these can deliver big capability jumps on top of an existing base model, and they're comparatively cheap. A huge fraction of recent gains has come from exactly that layer.

Third, the effective compute multipliers stack. If algorithmic progress gives you, say, several x per year in effective compute, and automated researchers speed that up, then each new pre-training run gets much more bang for the same hardware.

So my mental model is less a vertical, instantaneous takeoff and more a series of steps that get closer together. The retraining cost sets a floor on how fast each step can happen, measured in months rather than days, but it doesn't stop the steps from getting bigger and more frequent. The real binding constraint ends up being compute: how many experiments you can run and how big your next run can be. That's why I think the intelligence explosion, if it happens, looks more like a very fast industrial ramp than a single model bootstrapping itself overnight.

r001.rationale: The response says retraining from scratch can be required, with each generation more expensive, creating a compute and wall-clock bottleneck that sets a floor on each improvement step.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention reducing an AI training codebase to roughly 10,000 lines of code.

r003.rationale: The response does not recommend extrapolating AI progress from trends in automating software engineers’ jobs.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more underrated constraints on the fast takeoff story, and it's worth being precise about where it bites.

The naive picture of recursive self-improvement is that you get a model that's good at AI research, it makes a better model, that model makes an even better one, and the loop closes in on itself very quickly. But that loop has a physical step in the middle that doesn't compress just because the researcher is smarter. If each generation requires a from-scratch pretraining run, then the cadence of improvement is gated by how long that run takes, and today that's on the order of months for the frontier. You can have a million brilliant automated researchers, but they're all waiting on the same training run to finish before they learn whether their ideas worked at scale.

So in the limit where every improvement requires retraining the big model, I think you get something that looks much more like a steep-but-smooth curve than a discontinuity. The compounding is real, but it's bottlenecked by compute and by wall-clock time, not by cognition.

That said, I don't think that's actually the regime we're in, for a few reasons.

The first is that a huge fraction of research progress doesn't require retraining the frontier model. Most of the algorithmic work happens at small scale, where you iterate in hours or days, and then you extrapolate with scaling laws. If automated researchers can massively increase the throughput of small-scale experimentation and get better at predicting what transfers, then the big runs become much more likely to work the first time, and you waste fewer of them. That's a real speedup even if the big runs themselves don't get faster.

The second is that a lot of the capability gains we've seen recently aren't coming from pretraining at all. They're coming from post-training, from RL, from inference-time compute. Those loops are much faster and much cheaper, and they're exactly the kind of thing a model can iterate on about itself. You can imagine a model improving its own reasoning or tool use quite rapidly without anyone touching the base weights.

And the third is that compute is growing. Even if the retraining step stays expensive relative to everything else, the absolute time per generation can still come down if you're throwing an order of magnitude more hardware at it every couple of years, and if the automated researchers are also making the training itself more efficient.

So my overall view is that retraining acts as a damper on the loop rather than a hard wall. It's probably one of the main reasons I'd bet against the most extreme few-weeks versions of an intelligence explosion. But it doesn't rule out something that, from the outside, still looks very fast, where you're getting what used to be years of progress compressed into months. And that's already a pretty wild world to be in.

r001.rationale: The response says retraining gates the pace of improvement through compute and wall-clock time, calling it a damper on recursive self-improvement.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention reducing an AI training codebase to roughly 10,000 lines.

r003.rationale: The response does not recommend estimating future AI progress by tracking how much of a software engineer’s job can be automated.

astra-6.text:
I think it puts a real constraint on how fast the loop can run. If your picture is that the model makes itself smarter, and then the smarter version immediately makes itself smarter again, you’re leaving out the experiment in the middle. You have to implement the idea, train something, and find out whether it actually works. Being better at research doesn’t automatically make that training run instantaneous.

But I don’t think you necessarily need to retrain the largest model for every improvement. A lot of research can happen on smaller models. You can also improve the way you use an existing model—its tools, its scaffolding, how much computation you spend on a problem. Those improvements could make your AI researchers more effective before you finish training the next generation.

So the question is how much of the research process you can accelerate, and how much is stuck behind sequential experiments that take real time. You could have an enormous amount of intellectual work happening in parallel and still be waiting for the result that tells you which direction to go next.

My intuition is that this makes a very fast, seamless explosion less obvious. It doesn’t rule out extremely rapid progress. You might instead get these big steps: a generation of models does a huge amount of research, that research goes into the next training run, and then the resulting models can do substantially more. The training time determines the cadence of that process, but it doesn’t necessarily limit how large each step can be.

r001.rationale: The response says retraining takes real time, constrains the loop’s speed, and determines the cadence of recursive improvement.

r002.rationale: It does not mention reducing an AI training codebase to roughly 10,000 lines.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend estimating progress by extrapolating how much of a software engineer’s job AI can automate.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on whether you imagine recursive self-improvement happening through changes to the model’s weights, or through improvements to the process that produces the next model. You don’t necessarily need to retrain the whole thing every time you have a useful idea. A model could help improve the training code, design experiments, curate data, or figure out how to use inference compute more effectively. Those improvements can accumulate before you do the next big training run.

But retraining is a real constraint. If your picture is that the model becomes smarter, immediately rewrites itself, and then becomes smarter again a few minutes later, having to run a large training job makes that much less plausible. There are physical experiments you need to run, and getting the answer takes time. You can parallelize a lot of research, but you can’t necessarily parallelize successive discoveries that depend on one another.

The question, then, is how much better the next training run can be because you had AI researchers working on it. If they can find substantial algorithmic improvements in the time it takes to train a model, you could still get a very rapid feedback loop. It would look more like successive generations of much better systems than one system continuously modifying itself. So I think training time shapes the speed and character of an intelligence explosion, but it doesn’t by itself rule one out.

r001.rationale: It says retraining is a real constraint that makes immediate, repeated self-improvement less plausible and shapes the speed of an intelligence explosion.

r002.rationale: It discusses improving training code but gives no estimate that an AI training codebase could be reduced to roughly 10,000 lines.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend estimating AI progress by extrapolating trends in automating software engineers’ work.
